title: President Trump's Push to Reschedule Marijuana Hit a Snag. Is Green Thumb Still a Buy?
detail:
President Trump's Push to Reschedule Marijuana Hit a Snag. Is Green Thumb Still a Buy?
Jeff Siegel, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 11:20 AM MST 4 min read
NVDA
GTII.CN

Marijuana rescheduling was supposed to give U.S. cannabis companies some much-needed relief. Instead, another regulatory dispute threatens to drag out a process that's already taken years.

The latest complication involves a Government Accountability Office report examining how federal agencies evaluate controlled substances. Opponents of marijuana rescheduling want the report added to the administrative record, along with additional testimony and access to documents.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The DEA has indicated it doesn't object to including the report. But the additional requests could delay a final decision on moving marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III.

For Green Thumb Industries (OTC: GTBIF), the timing is frustrating, as rescheduling could eliminate a major federal tax burden and allow the company to keep more of the money it earns. That said, there's a stronger argument for owning Green Thumb than betting on what happens in Washington.

Image source: Getty Images.
The tax situation could change dramatically

Cannabis companies face an unusual disadvantage under Section 280E of the federal tax code. Because marijuana remains a Schedule I substance for much of the industry, businesses generally cannot deduct ordinary operating expenses such as employee salaries, rent, and advertising when calculating federal taxable income. Moving marijuana to Schedule III would eliminate that restriction for qualifying activities.

Green Thumb could benefit substantially, though the exact savings would depend on the final rules and how they're implemented. Until then, the company must continue operating under a tax structure that most other businesses don't face.

But even with that disadvantage, Green Thumb still generated $29 million in operating cash flow during Q2 2026. Revenue reached $306.7 million, while normalized earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) totaled $84.3 million. The company also reported $4.9 million in net income. Those results provide a useful glimpse of what Green Thumb is capable of, even in the absence of any broader federal tax relief.

The stock doesn't require a rescheduling victory

At approximately $6.40 per share, Green Thumb carries a market capitalization of around $1.4 billion, or roughly 1.1 times annualized second-quarter revenue. That's a relatively modest sales multiple for a company with an established retail network, positive earnings, and meaningful cash generation. The valuation also leaves room for improvement if the company can stabilize margins.

According to S&P Global's Global Market Intelligence, more than 80% of the companies in the S&P 500 index pay a dividend. Because the opportunity set is large, income-focused investing is a popular strategy among the retail crowd.

It makes sense why. Investing in growth stocks means betting on future earnings that may or may not materialize. Value investing, on the other hand, relies on the market eventually agreeing with your assessment of a particular bargain opportunity. There is uncertainty with these strategies.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Dividends provide a cash inflow to investors in up and down markets. And if you reinvest these distributions, it can boost the total return.

But it's important to understand that not all dividends are created equal. It all depends on the business that's backing them. Two consumer stocks help explain this line of thinking.

Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO) shares pay a dividend yield of 2.3%. Nike (NYSE: NKE) stock pays a dividend yield of 4.4%. Here's why only one of these dividend stocks is a better buy in October.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Both companies have remarkable dividend streaks

It's a good idea to first establish why these companies are elite at returning capital to shareholders. They both have incredible dividend streaks going right now.

Coca-Cola has raised its dividend for 64 consecutive years. That makes it a Dividend King, a business with at least 50 straight years of dividend increases.

That streak says nothing of the magnitude of the hikes. In the past decade, the beverage stock's dividend has grown by 51%.

Nike has raised its dividend for 24 straight years. That's a shorter streak than Coca-Cola's, but still an impressive one. If history is any indication, the sportswear company will raise the payout later this year.

Nike's dividend growth has been better than Coca-Cola's. The former's payouts have risen by 128% over the last 10 years.

It depends on what you care about most

When choosing which of these two stocks is the better buy in October, investors need to take some critical information into account. It comes down to business quality.

Both Coca-Cola and Nike possess wide economic moats. The soft drink giant has one of the strongest brands on Earth that drives customer loyalty and pricing power. The sportswear leader, which has admittedly struggled in recent years, has also been a globally recognized brand for decades.

title: History Says Nvidia Stock Does This in November. Here's the 1 Thing That Could Break the Pattern.
detail:
History Says Nvidia Stock Does This in November. Here's the 1 Thing That Could Break the Pattern.
Neil Patel, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 9:51 AM MST 5 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia's (NASDAQ: NVDA) rapid ascent to the world's most valuable enterprise might be unlike anything the market has ever seen. In the past five years, its share price has produced an incredible 899% gain (as of Oct. 15). With that return, a $10,000 investment would be worth $100,000 today.

The driver of this has been, unsurprisingly, artificial intelligence (AI). Nvidia's graphics processing units are the leading chips for training and running AI models. And these hardware devices are a hot commodity among the company's customers. Nvidia's data center revenue soared 117% year over year to $89 billion last fiscal quarter (Q2 2027 ended July 26).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

A burgeoning industry position in the middle of a generational technology shift is an easy sell to investors right now. History says this AI stock tends to perform well in November, so maybe now is a good time to buy shares. But there's one thing that could break that pattern of positive returns.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
November 2025 was the only negative return

This decade, Nvidia has been a compelling portfolio addition in November. In November 2020, shares were up 7%. In November 2021 and 2022, they jumped more than 25%. November 2023 saw a 15% increase, followed by a more muted 4% gain in November 2024.

The bears finally cheered last year. During the 11th month of 2025, Nvidia stock dipped 13%.

Nvidia optimists will take the average return of 13% and conclude that the share price will rise by that much this November. On the other hand, the naysayers will point to the clear deterioration in the stock's monthly performance in recent years. They'll assume shares are set to fall in November.

Investors shouldn't jump to any conclusions, however. The macroeconomic backdrop, as well as industry conditions, seem to have been anything but stable. Then there's market sentiment, which is constantly shifting based on how the investment community is feeling at any particular moment. November could bring anything.

Hyperscalers are Nvidia's key demand driver

Let's still assume that there's a higher probability that Nvidia posts a positive return compared to a loss in November. Instead of taking a victory lap, consider what could break that pattern of upbeat results. In my view, it comes down to one thing.

Nvidia's most important customer cohort contains the five big hyperscalers. Combined, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta Platforms, and Oracle, as well as other hyperscalers, contributed $49 billion to data center segment sales, which as mentioned, totaled $89 billion in the most recent fiscal quarter. These customers are spending tremendous sums of capital to build AI-related technical infrastructure.

On Nov. 13, Costco Wholesale (NASDAQ: COST) will issue a dividend payout to all of its shareholders on record as of Oct. 30. That dividend payout will be $1.47 per share.

That said, this payout in and of itself isn't enough of a reason to buy shares before October ends. The dividend payout only yields 0.6%, and there are plenty of other stocks in the consumer goods space that pay more. For instance, Coca-Cola's dividend yield is 2.3%, Procter & Gamble's is 2.7%, and PepsiCo's is 4.6%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Still, the reason someone might want to consider taking a position in Costco sooner rather than later is that its stock price has a history of outperforming the S&P 500, and Costco can continue to reward shareholders in three distinct ways.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Three ways to make money

As a retail chain, Costco often has a reputation for being a standard consumer goods company. It's also, however, a growth stock, with plenty of opportunities to expand domestically and internationally, building an even larger base of loyal customers and generating even more revenue.

For its fiscal 2025, Costco finished the year with 914 warehouses, expanding that to 939 by the end of fiscal 2026. For its fiscal 2027, it expects 967 warehouses to be open by year-end. With further expansion that can lead to increased revenue, investor enthusiasm can also increase, pushing the stock price higher. While Costco's stock price has returned 13.4% this year, slightly better than the S&P 500's 13.1% return over the same period, Costco has historically shown the ability to handily outperform the broader market.

Over the past five years, Costco's shares have risen 116%, while the S&P 500 has risen 73%. Of course, history is just a guidepost, but finding a stock that has demonstrated the ability to beat the broader markets over a five-year stretch can help build long-term wealth.

Two different dividend payouts

There isn't a set schedule of when it happens, but Costco has rewarded investors over the years with a special dividend. The last time it paid one out was in 2024, at $15 per share. Before that, it paid out a $10 dividend in 2020.

Finally, that brings us back to where we started, with the quarterly dividend. As mentioned earlier, a yield of 0.6% may not seem significant. Still, over time, as you add up Costco's stock price appreciation potential, special dividends, and quarterly dividends, it can offer significant total return potential for long-term shareholders.

title: Warren Buffett's Market Warning Is Hard to Ignore. But I'd Buy These 3 Stocks Anyway.
detail:
Warren Buffett's Market Warning Is Hard to Ignore. But I'd Buy These 3 Stocks Anyway.
James Brumley, The Motley Fool
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 8:37 AM MST 7 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Stocks continue to test record highs. But every bullish step forward pushes the market closer to a correction, if not a full-blown bear market.

That's the interpretation of the so-called Warren Buffett indicator at this time, anyway. The ratio comparing the total market cap of the U.S. stock market (as measured by the combined value of the Wilshire 5000's companies) to the nation's gross domestic product, or GDP, currently stands at a record high of 237.5%. It's a sign that stocks are dangerously overvalued.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

For perspective, this indicator only peaked at 138.5% at the height of the dot-com mania in early 2000, and barely and briefly eclipsed 100% in 2007, right before the subprime mortgage meltdown upended the rest of the domestic economy. Warren Buffett also recently commented in an interview with CNBC that "prices for an awful lot of things will look very silly." Investors have good reason to be concerned.

Still, the backdrop doesn't necessarily dictate whether or not you invest, but how you invest. There are always stocks worth owning. It's just a matter of figuring out which names those are, given the environment at the time. To this end, here's a closer look at three stocks to consider buying now regardless of Buffett's warning.

Warren Buffett. Image source: The Motley Fool.
Pfizer

It's no secret why Pfizer (NYSE: PFE) shares have struggled since peaking in late 2021. The wind-down of the COVID-19 pandemic simply ended overwhelming demand for its Paxlovid treatment, as well as for its vaccine co-developed with BioNTech. That year's revenue of just over $100 billion has since fallen back to its pre-pandemic annual norm of around $60 billion, with the impending expiration of its patents on Eliquis, Ibrance, Xtandi, and its pneumonia vaccine Prevnar 13 threatening roughly one-third of its current drug portfolio and weighing on the stock in the meantime.

Investors may be so fixated on Pfizer's past, however, that they're ignoring its promising future.

Granted, the crux of this bright future is still well down the road. Although the pharmaceutical company hopes to eventually have at least eight blockbuster oncology drugs in its portfolio, doubling the number of cancer patients it's currently serving, the drugmaker also knows this effort isn't likely to reach its full revenue stride until 2030. That's quite a wait, even for the most patient of shareholders.

Should You Invest in the S&P 500 Right Now or Wait? There's 1 Clear Answer

NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has generated an average annual total return of about 10% since its inception in 1957. However, the index has also gone through some wild swings over the past seven decades -- and those downturns shook out many long-term investors.

Over the past 12 months, the S&P 500 has risen 15% and trades just 2% below its all-time high. It also trades at 21 times forward earnings, compared to its average forward multiple of 17 for the past 25 years. Those numbers suggest it might not be the best time to invest in the S&P 500 via an exchange-traded fund (ETF) such as Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

However, the S&P 500 has also consistently rewarded investors who simply tuned out the near-term noise, stayed invested through downturns, and focused on the long-term gains. So should you invest in the S&P 500 today, even though it looks historically expensive?

Why is the S&P 500 such a resilient investment?

The S&P 500 includes the 500 largest companies in the United States. To join that elite club, they must have a market cap of at least $22.7 billion, have been profitable for at least the past four quarters, and have adequate liquidity and trading volume.

A company can't join the index until 12 months after its IPO, and at least 10% of its shares must be publicly traded. It also excludes certain companies -- including master limited partnerships (MLPs), business development companies (BDCs), and closed-end funds (CEFs) -- which don't issue common stock.

The S&P 500 rebalances itself quarterly to add rising stars and prune its laggards, and adjusts their weights based on their market caps. Over the long term, most actively managed funds struggle to outperform the S&P 500's automated indexing strategy.

That's why Vanguard's founder, John Bogle, advised investors to simply "buy the haystack" instead of searching for individual needles. Today, the S&P 500's biggest components include Nvidia (8.4% of the index), Apple (7.4%), Microsoft (5.8%), Amazon (3.7%), and Alphabet (3.1%). That makes it an easy way to gain instant exposure to the country's top companies without having to do too much homework on each stock.

But is there a "right" time to invest in the S&P 500?

The S&P 500 is a balanced investment for long-term investors, but they must be able to withstand double-digit drawdowns without panicking. Over the past two decades, the S&P 500 experienced peak-to-trough declines of 57% from Oct. 2007 to March 2009, 34% from Feb. to March 2020, and 25% from Jan. 2022 to Oct. 2022.

title: Is Solana Too Cheap to Ignore at Today's Prices?

Emma Newbery, The Motley Fool

BTC-USD
NVDA
Trade Solana on Coinbase

Crypto prices are starting to recover after a year-long slump, and analysts -- some of whom make a living out of predicting the crypto weather -- think the clouds may finally be clearing.

The lead crypto Bitcoin has soared 28% in the past three months as of Oct. 16. Its cousin, Solana (CRYPTO: SOL), gained 40% over the same period, but the popular altcoin is still trading 65% below last year's all-time high.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

When an asset has fallen so dramatically, it's important to understand why and ask whether it still has legs. In Solana's case, the abysmal price performance does not reflect its ecosystem growth, transaction revenues, or evolving role in stablecoins and real-world asset tokenization, which are key long-term drivers for blockchain usage. That makes it an interesting prospect at its current price of around $105.

Solana's thriving ecosystem

Solana's most-talked-about quality is its speed. It is significantly faster than Ethereum and, in theory, can rival Visa in terms of transactions processed per second.

But I'm more excited about another metric: on-chain fees.

Why? Because it shows that people are paying to use Solana's blockchain. At the time of this writing, Solana had generated more fees than any other chain in the past 30 days. Solana's low fees make soaring revenue a clear sign of very high transaction volumes.

Another sign of Solana's strong use case is that established businesses are using it. For example, Samsung recently announced Solana would be one of its partners as it rolled out USDC stablecoin access through its Samsung Wallet.

Solana still doesn't hold a torch to leader Ethereum in terms of the amount of stablecoins on its chain, but its stablecoin issuance is growing -- it recently hit an all-time high of $16.5 billion.

Solana is also a key player in real-world asset tokenization -- using blockchain tokens to represent ownership of assets such as equities or bonds. It ranks third by total value of tokenized assets on its chain. This month, stock tokenization veteran Securitize rolled out Securitize Stocks on Solana with tokenized versions of 12 U.S. megacap stocks.

In short, the crypto price slump has not stopped Solana's growth. However, success is not guaranteed. Not only is Solana susceptible to the ebbs and flows of crypto sentiment, but its 2025 high was also driven by a spike in meme coin activity, the likes of which we may not see again. Unlike Bitcoin, which has gained some traction as a form of digital gold, Solana's growth depends on adoption and, as with any emerging technology, it isn't yet clear how this will evolve.
